title: What Is AI? Rules and Learning
subtitle: Rules, search, learning from examples and language.
scenario: A smart home that decides when to turn its heating on.

sections.title: Programming a fixed rule
sections.problem: A thermostat turns the heating on below 19°C.
sections.concept: A classical program follows an explicit condition. It does not learn when the occupant likes heating.
sections.example: At 18°C the condition is true; at 21°C it is false.
sections.code:
temperature = 18
heating = temperature < 19
print('ON' if heating else 'OFF')

sections.title: Search is not the same as learning
sections.problem: A maze solver searches for an exit.
sections.concept: A search algorithm explores possible moves according to rules, even without training data.
sections.example: From a starting square, check legal neighbours until a path to the exit is found.

sections.title: Learning from examples
sections.problem: A heating log records temperature, time of day and user ON/OFF choices.
sections.concept: A supervised classifier fits a prediction rule from labelled examples. In contrast, clustering discovers groups without labels; reinforcement learning uses reward feedback.
sections.example: Training observations at 17°C → ON, 18°C → ON, 22°C → OFF suggest a temperature boundary.

sections.title: Language as input
sections.problem: A chatbot receives the sentence 'Turn the heating off'.
sections.concept: Natural language processing includes tokenisation, numerical representations and learned language models. Tokenising splits text into units; it does not by itself understand the instruction.

lab.context: Teach an image model with two classroom objects, then compare it with a fixed-rule thermostat.
steps: Predict one Quick, Draw! guess before it finishes.
Train two object categories in Teachable Machine without photographing people.
Run the small nearest-prototype Python notebook; change two training examples.
Record one misleading prediction and explain why it occurs.
lab.research: Compare fixed threshold and supplied learned classifier on a new heating CSV and explain any disagreement.

homework.context: A family's heating controller is still hard-coded to switch on below 19°C. A month of recorded preferences could make it more personal.
homework.mandatory: Implement the fixed thermostat rule and test it at 17°C, 19°C and 22°C.
homework.homework: Use a supplied trained ID3 component to learn from a simple heating decision log; plot predictions. You are not required to implement ID3 from scratch yet.

advanced: Find two different functions that agree on the same training examples.
Explain why a model can be correct on the sample but wrong elsewhere.

title: Supervised Learning: ID3
subtitle: Learn a tree by asking the most informative questions.
scenario: Predict whether the school can hold an outdoor activity from recorded weather decisions.

sections.title: From labelled examples to questions
sections.problem: Each record contains sky, wind, temperature and an answer (yes/no).
sections.concept: ID3 learns a categorical decision tree by selecting a feature question at each node.
sections.example: If all rainy examples are 'no', the rainy branch needs no more questions.

sections.title: Entropy: how mixed is a group?
sections.problem: Four answers are YES and four are NO.
sections.concept: Entropy measures uncertainty in the class distribution: a pure group has entropy 0; a balanced binary group has entropy 1 bit.
sections.code:
from math import log2
p = .5
print(-p*log2(p)-(1-p)*log2(1-p))

sections.title: Information gain and a greedy tree
sections.problem: Splitting on 'sky' separates a pure rainy group from a mixed sunny group.
sections.concept: Gain = parent entropy − weighted child entropy. ID3 chooses the unused feature with the greatest gain locally.
sections.example: With three yes and five no, parent H≈0.9544; split on sky leaves H≈0.4056; gain≈0.5488.

sections.title: Predictions and unknown categories
sections.problem: The tree has never seen the value 'foggy'.
sections.concept: A learned tree is not automatically reliable outside the categories observed in training. State the fallback policy explicitly.
sections.example: An unseen value can produce 'unknown' or a documented majority-class fallback.

lab.context: Build the same outdoor-activity classifier by hand and in Python.
steps: Predict whether sky or wind will be the best first question.
Calculate the gain for every root feature.
Run a categorical ID3 notebook and compare its learned tree.
Remove one example and predict it as a held-out case.
lab.research: Test the learner on an unseen category and explain how your fallback behaves.

homework.context: The school must decide whether to move an outdoor activity indoors when weather changes.
homework.mandatory: Compute the information gain of at least two feature tests.
homework.homework: Load the provided weather decisions, fit the supplied ID3 code and trace three unseen examples.

advanced: Construct an exact tree on eight training rows.
Show that perfect training fit does not determine an unseen label.

title: Unsupervised Learning: K-Means
subtitle: Find groups in data when no class labels have been supplied.
scenario: Group delivery locations so a courier can plan collection areas.

sections.title: No labels: a different learning problem
sections.problem: A map contains ten delivery coordinates but none are assigned to a district.
sections.concept: Unsupervised algorithms look for structure in unlabelled data. K-Means groups points by proximity to representative centres.
sections.example: The same six points could be split into two clusters without any human-provided A/B labels.

sections.title: Distance and centroid
sections.problem: A courier needs a representative centre for nearby addresses.
sections.concept: The centroid is the coordinate-wise average of points in a cluster. Euclidean distance measures straight-line separation.
sections.code:
group = [(1,1),(2,1),(2,2)]
print(tuple(sum(p[i] for p in group)/len(group) for i in (0,1)))

sections.title: The K-Means loop
sections.problem: Initial centres are placed at (1,1) and (9,8).
sections.concept: Repeat assignment to the nearest centre, then update each centroid, until assignments or centres stop changing.
sections.example: After one round, the first three points cluster near (1.67,1.33) and the other three near (8.33,7.67).
steps: Assign each point to its nearest centre

sections.title: What K-Means cannot tell you
sections.problem: Two groups of homes are clustered, but one road between them is closed.
sections.concept: Distance alone cannot account for every real-world constraint. Different K or random starts may change clusters; clusters are not true labels.
sections.example: A U-shaped group can be split unnaturally by simple distance-to-centroid decisions.
sections.code: print('K = 2 is a choice, not an automatically correct answer')

lab.context: A city courier wants two collection zones from six delivery coordinates.
steps: Plot six delivery points on a grid.
Manually calculate the centre for one proposed cluster.
Open the K-Means visualisation; change the starting centres.
Run the supplied notebook and compare its final grouping to your guess.
lab.research: Find a point arrangement where K=2 produces a misleading grouping.

homework.context: A parcel service is deciding where to place two collection points for neighbourhood deliveries.
homework.mandatory: Calculate the centroid of three given locations.
homework.homework: Use the K-Means notebook to cluster new delivery addresses and produce a labelled scatterplot.

title: Revision: Supervised and Unsupervised Learning
subtitle: Compare ID3, K-Means and K-nearest neighbours on one small dataset.
scenario: A small sports club records player measurements and wants both groups and predictions.

sections.title: Which algorithm fits the question?
sections.problem: We want to predict a known category, or group players into unknown types.
sections.concept: ID3 and KNN are supervised classification; K-Means finds clusters without labels. The input and expected output determine the choice.
sections.example: Known labels available + predict a new player → KNN or ID3. No labels + discover groups → K-Means.

sections.title: K-nearest neighbours
sections.problem: A new runner has measurements similar to several known runners.
sections.concept: KNN predicts the most common label among the K closest training examples. Unlike K-Means, it requires labels.
sections.example: For nearest labels ['fast','fast','slow'] and K=3, prediction='fast'.

sections.title: A fair revision experiment
sections.problem: A clustering model seems better because its output looks visually attractive.
sections.concept: Compare each model against the question it was built to answer; clusters cannot be scored as class predictions without an additional label mapping.
sections.example: ID3 explains categorical decisions, KNN uses distances and labels, K-Means only returns groups.
steps: Explain which cannot solve a given task

lab.context: Try the same plotted observations with KNN voting and K-Means grouping.
steps: Label a few points with known categories.
Predict a new point with K=3 nearest neighbours.
Remove labels and group the points with K-Means.
Compare what each result answers, and inspect an ID3 classification trace.
lab.research: Investigate a dataset where the choice of K changes the KNN prediction.

homework.context: A school sports club must classify a new participant and separately group existing participants into training sessions.
homework.mandatory: Explain which method serves each of the two needs.
homework.homework: Modify the lab KNN code to classify new points and compare K=1 vs K=3.

advanced: Compare a KNN decision boundary with an ID3 threshold.
Explain why K-Means cluster IDs do not mean known classes.

title: Computer Vision: Images as Data
subtitle: From pixels and channels to simple visual transformations.
scenario: A school scanner needs to clean a photographed black-and-white worksheet.

sections.title: The picture is a grid of numbers
sections.problem: A photograph looks like a continuous image on screen.
sections.concept: A digital image is a rectangular grid of pixels. Grayscale pixels often range from 0 (black) to 255 (white).
sections.example: A 3×3 image is a table of nine intensity values; changing its centre affects one small square.

sections.title: Colours, channels and dimensions
sections.problem: A red pixel is not described by one intensity value.
sections.concept: RGB images store three channel values per pixel. A shape such as 64×64×3 records height, width and channels.
sections.example: Pure red may be represented as (255,0,0); black is (0,0,0).

sections.title: Thresholding and simple filters
sections.problem: Ink is dark and paper is bright in a scan.
sections.concept: Thresholding converts each value into light or dark. A small blur or edge-detection filter examines neighbouring pixels.
sections.code:
pixels = [80,140,230]
print([0 if p<128 else 255 for p in pixels])

sections.title: Seeing what changes
sections.problem: A scan becomes hard to read after over-aggressive filtering.
sections.concept: Preprocessing must preserve useful information. A clean result is not always one that looks more dramatic.
sections.example: A threshold of 250 may erase grey pencil strokes that were present at 180.
sections.code: print('Always keep the original image for comparison')

lab.context: Clean a fictional low-contrast worksheet photographed on a phone.
steps: Experiment with a tiny grayscale pixel grid.
Use an interactive filter to compare blur and edges.
Run the image notebook to convert pixels to black and white.
Explain which filter preserves the handwriting best.
lab.research: Implement a custom 3×3 edge kernel on a tiny matrix and show the result.

homework.context: A teacher wants to improve a photograph of homework so it is easier to read.
homework.mandatory: Apply a threshold to five pixel values.
homework.homework: Modify the supplied image-preprocessing notebook and show side-by-side images.
